summary: Gives recommendations from the IETF IPv6 Working Group to the 3GPP mobile standards community on how to use IPv6. These include allowing multiple prefixes per primary PDP context and not assigning one prefix to more than one primary PDP context.

plainLanguage.summary: Phone companies were writing rules for using the new internet addresses. This document is a friendly list of advice from the internet experts on how to set them up well.

subtitle: IPv6 usage recommendations from IETF to 3GPP mobile standards

tldr.problem: 3GPP mobile network standards were designed to assign a single IPv6 prefix and a single interface identifier per connection, which is incompatible with standard IPv6 behavior and prevents use of privacy addresses and modern IPv6 features.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF IPv6 Working Group recommends three changes: allow multiple prefixes per connection, assign each prefix to only one connection, and allow terminals to generate multiple interface identifiers including random ones.
tldr.outcome: The 3GPP standards body adopted these recommendations in 2002, making 3GPP networks compatible with standard IPv6 stacks and enabling features like privacy addresses and site renumbering.

today: RFC 3314 is Informational and has not been updated or obsoleted. The 3GPP standards adopted its recommendations in 2002, incorporating them into releases 99, 4, and 5 of TS 23.060. These recommendations remain the basis for IPv6 use in 3GPP mobile networks.

sections.title: Background and Cooperation
sections.content:
This document presents recommendations from the IETF IPv6 Working Group to the Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP), an international standards body for mobile telecommunications. In 2001, the IPv6 WG and 3GPP held a joint meeting to discuss how IPv6 should be used in 3G mobile networks, resulting in a design team that produced this document.

The IPv6 WG supports IPv6 adoption in 3GPP networks and offers recommendations in a spirit of open cooperation. Notably, 3GPP adopted the primary recommendations of this document at its March 2002 plenary meeting, applying them retroactively to earlier releases. The document is informational, not a standard, but represents the consensus of the IPv6 community on best practices for mobile networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet experts and the phone companies met and talked about new internet address rules. The internet experts wrote down their advice in this document. The phone companies liked the advice and started using it.

sections.title: PDP Contexts and IPv6 Addressing
sections.content:
A PDP Context is a 3GPP term for a connection between a mobile terminal and a gateway node (GGSN). Each primary PDP context acts as a point-to-point link, and the 3GPP system assigns one IPv6 address per connection. The original 3GPP design was restrictive: the GGSN would assign a single 64-bit interface identifier and advertise a single /64 prefix, forcing the mobile device to use exactly one IPv6 address.

The IPv6 addressing architecture, by contrast, is designed to allow hosts to generate multiple addresses from advertised prefixes and interface identifiers. IPv6 nodes are expected to support multiple addresses on a single link, use privacy addresses for anonymity, and participate in features like site renumbering by adapting to new prefixes. The original 3GPP model conflicted with these expectations, making standard IPv6 software incompatible with 3GPP networks.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone connection is like a wire to the internet. The old design said each wire gets exactly one address label. But real internet computers use multiple address labels on one wire, like having a mail box with several names. The new rules let phone networks work the same way.

sections.title: The Three Key Recommendations
sections.content:
The IPv6 WG makes three recommendations to 3GPP. First, the GGSN should advertise multiple IPv6 prefixes to each primary PDP context through standard IPv6 Router Advertisements. This allows terminals to participate in site renumbering and other mechanisms that depend on multiple prefixes. Second, each global or site-local prefix should be assigned to only one primary PDP context. This means a mobile device with multiple connections gets a different prefix per connection, simplifying routing and prefix tracking. Third, 3GPP nodes should be allowed to generate multiple interface identifiers within those prefixes, including randomly generated ones for privacy.

These changes have several benefits: laptops attached to 3GPP handsets will work without special drivers because they use standard IPv6 autoconfiguration; IPv6 implementations in handsets need no special 3GPP logic; applications gain access to different address types including private and site-scoped addresses; and the system becomes compatible with future IPv6 features.
sections.plainLanguage: The advice is three things: (1) give multiple address labels per wire, (2) don't give the same label to two wires, and (3) let devices make up extra labels if they want secret ones. This way, phones and computers use the same rules.

sections.title: Addressing a Scale Concern
sections.content:
A natural concern when assigning a full /64 prefix to each primary PDP context is whether IPv6 address space would become exhausted. The RFC addresses this using the Host Density Ratio (HD), a measure of practical address assignment efficiency derived from actual telephone and data network allocations. Assuming an HD ratio of 0.8 and using only the portion of IPv6 space designated for global unicast addresses, the calculation shows that approximately 490 trillion /64 prefixes are assignable.

This translates to around 80,000 PDP contexts per person on Earth today. Even accounting for IPv6 prefixes used by non-3GPP networks, the address space is demonstrably sufficient. The document cites related IETF and regional addressing authority policies to support this conclusion, confirming that /64 prefix allocation per connection poses no practical exhaustion risk.
sections.plainLanguage: Could there be enough address labels for billions of phone connections? The math says yes: there are enough to give over 80,000 connections to every person on Earth. Even sharing with computers, there is plenty left.

sections.title: Practical Implementation Path
sections.content:
The RFC recommends a specific implementation approach: the GGSN maintains a pool of /64 prefixes for each Access Point Name (APN). At PDP context activation, the GGSN advertises one or more of these prefixes to the mobile device via standard Router Advertisements. Instead of tracking individual IPv6 addresses as in the original design, the SGSN (the mobility node) maintains a list of prefixes associated with each PDP context.

This approach requires minimal changes to existing 3GPP specifications and preserves all advantages of alternative solutions. Mobile devices are not required to be routers; they may use the /64 prefix for their own interfaces or share it with attached devices such as laptops. Duplicate Address Detection is handled locally by the device, without requiring network-side proxy DAD, keeping the system simple. The document also recommends that future IETF work define an "IPv6 over PDP Contexts" document to help developers implement IPv6 over 3GPP links.
sections.plainLanguage: Each phone connection gets a supply of address labels to hand out. When a phone connects, the network gives it some labels, and the phone figures out which labels to use. The phone does not have to be smart about managing the labels; it just uses them.
